utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you all. We trust that the accused is in better health at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness is now coming back into the court. Good afternoon. If I could remind you of the affirmation you took, which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the overhead projector be lowered, please. I'd like to ask the technical booth to do that so that I have visual contact with the witness. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, good afternoon. I shall carry on with my questions from where we left off last time, and I should now like to ask you to tell us what the role and tasks were of the 9th Military Naval Sector within the frame work of the naval district as a whole and the Adriatic coastal battlefront during the time of your first term of office as commander there, the sector.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the concept of the day of total national defence, or All People's Defence, which was in force and our general military doctrine, the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector was designed for defence purposes of the coast and an area in-depth within the littoral as well as anti-air attack at sea and providing security for the fleet and naval forces and acting in cohorts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the concept of total national defence and social self-protection, as it was called, of the SFRY at the time, did it start out from the premise that the state can be open to outside aggression or the NATO pact at the time? Did it envisage an outside enemy? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the assessments were always that one of the possible variants was an aggression either from the east or from the west. Those were the assumptions. And the danger was at the time of an internal conflict breaking out, in actual fact. And to a lesser degree was there the fear of a possible aggression from outside, an external aggression, although we never forgot such a possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, the concept of total national defence, All People's Defence, was it based upon the premise of an external, outside aggression or was it based on the possibility of an internal conflict? Which?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our concept, it was the external danger that was paramount, and we based it on that. As far as an internal one was concerned, we considered the situation in the country to be stable, and this was true until the 1980s, or the end of the 1980s, in actual fact, when there were signs already of certain instability within the country and the possibility of the conflict coming to a head.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The conception of total national defence, did it change at all? Did it undergo changes, or in 1990 was it the same? Did 1990 see the army with the same concept?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The concept didn't change. It remained the same, and it was always focused on this external enemy or danger from outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in line with these premises and this assumption of an outside enemy and aggression, were the units and commands trained in that direction, geared towards that objective?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And was it also in keeping with the premise of defence from an outside aggressor that the materiel and general resources were designed in that way, to defend the territory from an outside aggressor? Would that be true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, the SFRY, did it defend itself from the sea, thinking that it would be open to a NATO aggression, naval forces and airborne forces? Was that the principal anxiety?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We always focused on anti-air defence from the coast and the sea and especially individual sections which were the most -- most prone to airborne attacks of that kind, taking the NATO variant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, the organisation of the territory, did it begin from the hinterland around Dubrovnik for defence purposes against an outside enemy?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And was the main force geared towards defending that territory, did it have its headquarters in Trebinje? Was it in fact the Trebinje Brigade we discussed earlier on? Was that the fulcrum of support and -- for defence, the 72nd Trebinje Brigade, the one I had -- the 472nd Trebinje Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 472nd Trebinje Brigade was the basic point of support for a defence of the coastal belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what about the Konavle area? Yugoslav People's Army more than 20 years ago set this up as the first line of defence; is that right? Did it build up underground channels, warehouses and storage in order to put up a defence against forces that were far mightier, it was supposed would be far mightier?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The whole zone of defence was prepared for that eventuality, defence against an airborne attack along the coast and into the hinterland which comprised the sector zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So this hinterland region, it was also incorporated into this general line of defence; for example, the Konavle area and the other coastal belt areas; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The central line of defence from a possible attack from that side, from that axis, was it the Dalmatinska Ploce, the plateau with Mostar and Knin to the north?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the level of an army operation on the Adriatic coastal battleground or theatre of operation we expected the main line of defence to be at the Dalmatinska Ploce, or Dalmatian Plateau area, and exercises and training was also -- always conducted along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So in line with this general concept, was there a lot of military materiel, weapons, and technical resources stationed in the area beforehand, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would it be true to say that the weapons belonging to the JNA, which were later used in the wars that took place on the territory of the former Yugoslavia was not brought into the area of conflict but that the bulk of those weapons were already located in those areas? They were already there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the first conflicts, did they arise with respect to the fact that the JNA already had weapons and materiel in the area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand that question of yours. What do you mean, who used the weapons or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: My question was this: The first conflicts that took place on the territory of the SFRY, was the pretext, did they begin because the already existing weapons wished to be seized, the weapons that already existed there?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There is no date placed before the witness in which to frame any response. It is unclear how he can direct an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to place a date to your question, do Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you think, Mr. Rodic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour. We've discussed this general area, and the dates we're discussing are 1990, 1991, and 1992, which was the well-known dates relating to the conflict in the former SFRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it would help me at least if you could say what you saw or what you regard as the first conflicts on the territory of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me be more specific, more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: For example, in the autumn of 1991, does the witness know whether there were any attacks on military facilities, warehouses where weapons were stored in the area that we were discussing a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's not clear what area we're discussing, and if I could ask just to have that so that we can, if need be for redirect, frame a proper question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm talking about the area we -- we discussed in the previous few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's all very loose and general, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me put it this way, then:

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the conflicts or attacks on military facilities of this kind in the area of Southern Dalmatia during 1991, in the summer or autumn of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I wasn't occupying the position I occupied later in that area. I was partly in the Serbian government and partly I was in the countryside for two and a half months. I was out of active service, away from active service during that time. So all I can say was on the basis of what I read in the papers, and it was general knowledge, common knowledge that from time to time in certain regions of Croatia there were conflicts that broke out around the barracks and certain garrisons were blocked, weapons were seized. And weapons were also brought in over the black market through underground channels into the country. The papers wrote about that and there were drives to suppress that, to stop the import of weapons. I know that in Dalmatia the conflicts broke out in the Knin, Krajina area from where -- which is where the events actually were triggered, because the Serbs were opposed to accepting the new flag that was being flown and the Croatian forces of the Republic of Croatia, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. You were in the Ministry of Defence yourself of the Republic of Serbia, were you not, until July 1991. So I assume you were informed and aware of when the command post of the military naval district was moved from Split, out of Split. Roughly speaking. You don't have to give us an exact date.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- can't say exactly, but I think it was towards the end of July or in August, perhaps. I'm not quite sure. But I do know what took place in front of the military naval sector's department when the soldier in the tank was strangled, and I think that was in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could that have been May? May I jog your memory?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right; May.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So that makes it May 1991; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the command post of the military naval sector moved because it wasn't secure, it wasn't safe in Split?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was the main reason. It wasn't safe and secure to command from the town of Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So the forward command post of the naval military district, was it then located at Vis, the island of Vis?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. The command of the military naval district, the forward command post was sent to Vis and the stronghold there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And the wartime command post of the military naval district in Zernovica, was it taken over by the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The wartime command post in Zernovica was under a blockade for about two months, I believe, and after an agreement had been reached to -- about an exchange after some -- a lot of casualties and unrest, that command post was -- they left that command post about two months after the blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were all the naval communications attacked in the area around the islands and between the islands?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Certain batteries were taken control of on the islands and along the coast, radar stations in particular and other points of support and facilities that were there to defend the islands. There were also attacks on naval ships within the island belt.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After the attacks on the warehouses, barracks, and JNA facilities first in Slovenia and then in Croatia, did the leadership of the JNA envisage moving the -- that this could spread to the BH territory?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There is no evidence about Slovenia. The question has been Dalmatia right now. And further, if we could get some idea again of time frame. The question is remaining very general.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sure my learned colleague will remember that I started the cross-examination before the Easter break and there were two rather lengthy interruptions, intervals, and I think that already on the first day of the cross-examination we discussed this point, and the witness spoke about the attacks on the military facilities, the barracks, the family of the soldiers of the JNA in Slovenia and Croatia, and he spoke about what he knew. He told us what he knew about that and answered in the affirmative. So I'm just following on from those first questions that I asked the witness some time ago now and based on the answers he gave me then. I'm just following on from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, could you just answer that last question of mine. It is this: After those activities and what went on against the JNA on the territory of Slovenia and Croatia, did you happen to know whether the military leadership envisaged that these kinds of conflicts could be continued and spill over into Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, did the military leadership take any measures along those lines?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The general military assessments and evaluations indicated that the conflicts would certainly expand to Bosnia-Herzegovina, and as far as what was known about what was going on in the Dubrovnik zone and what we knew there, this was reflected in December 1991, towards the end of the year, on the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Because of the overall situation as it was, did the JNA have to carry out additional mobilisation? Because in peacetime, it had less personnel and also there were divisions according to republican affiliation.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mobilisation was carried out, and the response was rather poor. So that caused problems. There was always a shortage of personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that personnel needed in order to keep the technical equipment and the communication areas that the JNA was defending?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please give me your opinion, if possible. The tasks and objectives of the JNA units that were on the move in the Dubrovnik area, and was all of that supposed to be interpreted from the point of view of the unity objectives and tasks of the JNA in the entire area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as this specific theatre is concerned, the Dubrovnik part, then it should be said that the units that were mobilised and prepared then and at such levels at that and involving such a number of personnel could not only serve the purpose of defending facilities but, rather, an operation with a certain operative objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Movements of the JNA towards Mostar and reaching Slano on the Adriatic coast as well as the naval blockade of Dubrovnik, were all of these elements of an overall operation carried out by the JNA in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. accordance with the SFRY constitution?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. This operation, the Dubrovnik operation, was certainly conceived within the context of a strategic operation for the entire territory of Croatia by which the Supreme Command or, rather, the General Staff intended to paralyse the Croatian paramilitary formations or defence forces and to deblock all the imperiled garrisons and prevent the organisation of the Croatian forces for any significant type of assault operations. This area was actually part of Southern Croatia, and it fitted into this single strategic operation conceived.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I would just like to explain one more thing. You yourself said the Dubrovnik operation, and this is an expression that is often used, the "Dubrovnik operation," "the Dubrovnik campaign," or "the campaign against Dubrovnik." Was that really the objective of that operation that we discussed a few minutes ago? Was its objective the town of Dubrovnik itself as a city or did it have to do with something different?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this name, the Dubrovnik operation, is one that can be used only conditionally. Sometimes it is referred to as "the so-called Dubrovnik operation," but Dubrovnik was not its objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective went all the way to Mostar and the Neretva River valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in relation to the single operation of the JNA throughout Yugoslavia, were all units commanded by the General Staff on the basis of the orders of the Presidency of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: According to the SFRY constitution, was it the obligation and duty of the JNA to protect the territorial integrity of the country and its constitutional order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the constitutional framework within which the JNA operated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind what was said previously about the very concept of general people's defence, what we discussed about awhile ago, as well as the period that was close to the period of your first command in the 9th Military Sector, can you tell me briefly what changed in this role and task of the 9th Military Sector when you came for the second time on the 7th of October, 1991, to head this sector? What changed in relation to the previous tasks?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation had changed radically. Combat operations started on the 1st of October. Certain elements within the zone of defence were threatened, and also there was a conceived operative objective from the level of the Supreme Command. A decision was reached to organise an operation which would curb these threats, and that is what was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were these changes varied then and quite radical as compared to the previous period of your command in the 9th Military Naval Sector?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. Of course. The first period was a period of peace, it was in peacetime, and that is when preparations were carried out for possible action in a stable state, a united state by all accounts, whereas this was the beginning of an internal conflict which threatened to turn into a larger-scale war.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was the command of the 9th VPS trained to carry out the tasks that were given to the sector in the second half of 1991? And I'm primarily referring to combat actions on land. That is what I primarily have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the 9th Sector was, I think, very well trained to use all its formation forces in a possible war that could have been expected.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When I asked you this I meant the differences in relation to the previous period when you were commander of the 9th VPS from 1983 to 1989. According to that concept, the 9th VPS could have expected an attack from sea, and the 9th VPS was trained to respond to that kind of attack. So this response would be aimed at the sea, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 9th Sector was trained for all its specific tasks involved in a possible war within its area of responsibility. So that does not involve only defence from the sea but also carry out combat operations on land.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at the command staff exercises, did you and your sector train such land operations, that is to say the type of operations that actually took place in October through December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We carried out exercises, command staff exercises, tactical exercises on -- and operational exercises on land against an aggressor attacking our country, and we were practising both offensive and defensive types of action. However, we never trained and never had exercises for any kind of operations within an internal conflict, as was the one that took place towards the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not prepared for that. Not only we, but all other commands too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know exactly when the 2nd Operational Group was established and out of which operational and tactical units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know when the command of the 2nd Operational Group was established, and that was sometime in mid-September 1991, a bit before the 15th of September. The units were being prepared, mobilised, and brought into the zone of operations depending on their level of combat readiness, and I can give the names of the units if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This is the way I'm going to phrase my question: What about the 37th Corps? Do you know which unit it belonged to before it became part of the organisational set-up of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was within the military district, either the Belgrade or the Skopje military district. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was it perhaps the 1st Military District, with its headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the 1st Military District, with its headquarters in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the 2nd Corps? Before it became part of the 2nd Operational Group was it within the Skopje military district in Macedonia, with its headquarters in Skopje?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The command and the staff of the 2nd Operational Group, were they established from among the officers of the inspectorate and the centre of higher military schools?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of the officers came from the main inspectorate of the JNA, then also the centre of higher military schools in Belgrade, and some came from Podgorica too, from the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, as a commander of the military district of Boka for many years, did you ever hear of, learn of, or personally take part in a single exercise in the General Staff or anywhere else where the establishment of the 2nd Operational Group was practised, taught, and the deployment of its units and -- the operational deployment of its units and the general conduct of such an operation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not, specifically speaking of the 2nd Operational Group, but the exercises that take place cannot be identical to any possible situation. However, there are always some assumptions, concepts, schematics that are envisaged, and we did have some exercises involving the establishment of operational groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I meant specifically the 2nd Operational Group and the type of operations -- the type of tasks that it carried out.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, not that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The objection would have gone to time frame and the fact that the witness gave a time for when the operational group he believed was formed. The question was not phrased in such a way that it could have been answered according to his previous answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the witness was coping fairly well, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Ms. Somers. I think you can carry on, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed so I don't forget what I wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead, but when I asked you about your personal participation and knowledge regarding any kind of exercises, I meant specifically training the establishment of the 2nd Operational Group, the deployment of the commands and units of this group, operational activities and general activities related to that operational group and with specific reference to what it actually did in the autumn of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All exercises that were carried out by the Yugoslav People's Army, staff exercises, joint exercises at all levels, were carried out on the basis of certain variants of the war plan. So it's aggression coming either from the east or from the west. In our war plan, we never provided for an internal conflict, absolutely not, especially to the degree that we saw actually happen. So we couldn't train the establishment of this kind of operational group at all, like the 2nd Operational Group, in fact, with the composition of the units as was established in September 1991, and especially with the tasks that that operational group was assigned at the beginning of October or, rather, the 1st of October, 1991. So quite definitely we did not train this variant for the command of the 2nd Operational Group for the reasons that I have stipulated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Operational Group, then, and its command, was it a temporary strategic and operative establishment which had not existed previously in that zone and area of responsibility or having that role at all?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: While you were the Minister of Defence in the Republic of Serbia, did you ever hear of the preparations of an operational group of this kind at all?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, something was formed at the time. Whether it was September or -- but it was the first operational group that was established in Croatia, Lika, Banja, Kordun, that general region. The first operational group was formed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, in general frameworks how much time would be needed for the successful planning and equipping of a strategic operation, an operation of a strategic level and strategic importance?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you need basic prerequisites. All the rest is hypothetical.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, my question is a hypothetical. I'm asking you hypothetically speaking.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we have an enemy on an equal footing, if I can put it that way, and not an internal conflict, then far more time would be needed. At least a month. Between one and two months would be needed for a strategic operation at the level of an operational group numbering three to four corps within it. In a classical conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me in principle, please, what the preparation of a relatively major military operation would entail.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be composed of several operational actions, the planning of the operation itself, planning the forces necessary, bringing in the forces and troops and organising them. Of course, this would mean mobilisation, first of all, bringing in the men and organising them according to the branches, services, objectives, goals, et cetera. The introduction of those forces, those troops into the regions and areas of operation depending on where they were being brought in from. Preparations would entail training for operations and training for expected attacks, organising joint action of the branches and services to be deployed and to take part in any given operation. Support and reinforcements must be provided for as well, and preparation of the command posts and command staffs themselves, the formation of new commands, subordination and detachment of units; that kind of thing. And hand-in-hand with that, of course, would be preparations for the staffs and the commands given the operation itself. Combat documents would be required, and the compiling of directives, orders, combat orders, and so on and so forth with the individual stages of the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, who would be in charge of preparing operations of this kind, roughly speaking? Whose role would that be?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we're talking about the strategic level operation, then it is the General Staff that does that for the portion which it is responsible for, that is to say the highest ranking documents, the orders for the establishment, structuring of the command to lead the operation, the compiling of directives, et cetera. All the other things would be done lower down, the command which was entrusted with the operation itself, which means the command of the operational group, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, whether the command of the 2nd Operational Group in this instance, bearing in mind your knowledge, experience, and so on from the material period, October, November, December 1991, had the time, the staff, the technology necessary to plan such an operation successfully, the one that began on the 1st of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the operation was envisaged and the troops set up for it to become operational, it did not have the objective prerequisites for it being a success, for successfully preparing and organising such an operation and putting it into practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what about the 9th VPS, the 9th Military Naval Sector? That's something you know about perhaps best during that period of time. The ground forces that your sector had within its composition when you arrived to head it on the 7th of October, 1991. You don't have to give me precise dates, but I'm interested in learning of the changes that took place in that respect. What was the dynamics of those changes, that is to say which units belonging to the ground forces did you encounter? Where were they deployed to? When did they go and return to your own establishments, and so on and so forth? So I don't need the exact dates, but can you just briefly explain the dynamics of all this, how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is beyond a compound question. There are five or six subquestions in there. If counsel is trying to elicit answers, if he could break it down I think it would probably be easier to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is a very complex line that you're posing this question along, Mr. Rodic. I think I can see generally what you're getting at, but it would be more manageable, as Ms. Somers suggests, if you were able to break it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try, Your Honour. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But then please be brief in your answers. Mr. Jokic, tell me please, when you arrived on the 7th of October, 1991, what ground forces were within the 9th Military Naval Sector, the 9th VPS? Which land forces or ground forces did you encounter within the composition of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from what the sector actually had establishment-wise under it, as far as the infantry sections are concerned, the sector just had the 4th Battalion within it, which was already pulled out of the combat and prepared to go back to within the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: After that were there any changes in these infantry units within the composition of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 9th Sector received some peripheral companies for control and clearing up of the territory and providing guards and security, and it worked together with them until the 21st of October. After that, on the 21st of October, it received the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade until the 25th of October. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 25th of October, the 472nd Brigade was attached, which was on the 6th of November to have been pulled out. However, this was prolonged until the 21st of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And tell me, please, just to interrupt you there for a moment, when the 472nd Motorised Brigade once again came under the command of the 9th VPS during this period of time, the period you're mentioning, the 25th of October and the 21st of November, 1991, what happened to the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade? Did it step outside your composition, your troops, or not?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade on the 25th of October went on leave, following a regulation that was in force at the time, and on the 6th of November it replaced the 2nd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade in the region across the Dubrovacka Rijeka, and from that time on it was within the composition permanently of the 9th Sector as a temporarily attached subordinated unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, on the 21st of November, the 472nd Motorised Brigade entered within the composition of the 2nd Corps, become part and parcel of the 2nd Corps without the 3rd Battalion which remained within the 9th VPS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the meantime, was a mixed detachment of the TO established at any point?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the request of the command of the 2nd Operational Group, the need to have a battalion go to Slano. And for that reason and also because of certain incidents that had taken place in the region, I established a mixed detachment of the Territorial Defence which was replaced [as interpreted] by the 4th Battalion of the 472nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. To clarify, the admiral said that he formed the mixed detachment which replaced, not "was replaced" but "replaced," which replaced the 4th Battalion. It said in the transcript that -- "which was replaced." It should say which replaced the battalion of the 472nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, something about the 3rd Light Brigade. What happened to that? Did it come within the composition of the 9th VPS? Did it step down from the 9th VPS? What happened to the 3rd Light Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 3rd Light Brigade became part of the [Realtime transcript read in error "6th"] 9th Military Naval Sector on the 6th of November, 1991, and it was to have replaced in part the 472nd Brigade in its area of operation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I believe there is a transcript error. It says the 3rd Light Brigade became part of the 6th Naval Sector. I believe it was 9th. If we could just get that clarified, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure what was intended was 9th. We will treat it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true that some of the territorial units which you mentioned, that they also left the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And that they went to join up with other formations. Some perhaps went home, others were disbanded. Can you tell us a bit about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The 2nd Tactical Group was not under my command, for example, if you had that in mind. And it was disbanded. It had two brigades and two companies of transporters and a tank company. They were disbanded and returned to their original formation. And then they were -- two units of the Territorial Defence of Trebinje were added to the 9th Military Naval Sector on the 6th of November, and they were the TO battalion and the TO detachment of Trebinje. And they had the task in their own region to replace the units of the 472nd Brigade as of the 6th of November onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Changes in organisation that took place so frequently and in the establishment of the sector, especially of units belonging to the army, to the ground forces, did all of this have an adverse effect on the system of command that you had?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Temporary subordination, being under certain commands for a while and then leaving one's own establishment, disbanding as such. All of that had a very negative effect on the combat use, commanding, control over combat operations, combat readiness, and generally speaking, on overall conduct and the effect of actions taken within the area of combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that this was only one of the problems related to command and control if one bears in mind mobilisation, the fact that a state of war was not proclaimed, that there is not enough trained personnel, that most of the troops consist of reservists and so on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is a set of problems that did have a negative effect on the overall situation regarding command and control.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the late commander, Admiral Djurovic, who headed the 9th VPS before you did, issued any kind of directives for attack, for assault operations to his units that would involve the 1st of October and that would spell out the objectives of the operation that actually faced the 9th Military Naval Sector, that is to say tasks and objectives that are to be carried out by the 9th Military Naval Sector as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I came after he was killed, when I came to the zone, to the command in Kumbor, I found his order to carry out an attack, to have the 9th Sector carry out an attack. In that order, the tasks of the sector were referred to. They were rather minor ones in relation to the overall tasks of the 2nd Operational Group in view of the fact that he had one battalion only.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Rodic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This order of his, was it in line with the directive that we saw here a few days ago that was written by the commander of the 2nd Operational Group and sent on to the chief of General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this order of his which, of course, elaborated the task that he had received from the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, and that task is specified there and it reads more or less as follows: Deblock the Prevlaka barracks, act in concert with the forces of the 2nd Tactical Group, act along the Debeli Brijeg-Plocice line, and take the region of Molunat and the region of Vitaljina all the way up to Prevlaka. That was it, roughly speaking, without giving an exact quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that the ultimate task of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This was the initial task. You asked what the task was that he had given, Admiral Djurovic. Well, that's the one. Later on, of course, after he got killed, other tasks followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how you understood this task of a blockade of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not receive this task to carry out a blockade of Dubrovnik. The task of blockading Dubrovnik was received by the command of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. That's not being challenged. The command of the 2nd Operational Group did get this task, but the units of the 9th VPS, did they take part in carrying out this task of a blockade of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat operations within the operations that are commanded by the 2nd Operational Group command were carried out every day in accordance with combat documents. I received every day since my arrival on the 8th of October, every day within this operation I received orders as to what the task of my units was on that particular day. If I need to go into that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Well, let me simplify it, then. In the period when you came to command the 9th VPS from the 7th of October until of 31st of December, 1991, was the blockade of Dubrovnik an ongoing, permanent task, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm saying once again that this task of the blockade of Dubrovnik is one that the 9th Sector never received. Its task was to take Cavtat, to take Kupari, to take Zupa, to take the fortresses, Rijeka Dubrovacka, and that entire sequence. But this kind of task, carry out a blockade of Dubrovnik, that is not a task that the sector ever received, nor was it one that it carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: According to the directive, there was this task of a blockade of the town of Dubrovnik from land and sea in order to prevent having weapons brought in, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That is undeniable. But again, I'm saying that this is the task that was received by the 2nd Operational Group, according to the directive, not the sector. Not in a single one of its documents did the sector receive this task of blocking Dubrovnik. Never. But from the sea, yes. Let me correct myself on that score. It was what Admiral Djurovic was told on the 1st of October. He was supposed to block the ports within the zone of Dubrovnik from the sea, and this task remained valid from when I came too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And how was the blockade of Dubrovnik from land carried out?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Rijeka Dubrovacka was taken along with the neighbourhoods in the Rijeka area, and when we entered Mokosica, Zaton Veli, Zaton Mali, it can be considered as the carrying out of a blockade of the town from land. That was towards the end of November. But I'm saying this yet again: This was the task of the 2nd Operational Group within which the 9th Sector was, along with its units. And it carried out its task within that context and covered with its units this zone that I referred to just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I agree that the task of the 2nd Operational Group was that, but not one man can carry out a task, it has to be the units that are within that group; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. That is why the command does have its units. And then these tasks are carried down the line, so to speak, so that they could carry them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was town blockade envisaged in the military doctrine of the JNA within the area of fighting for a specific town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course. In the doctrine, in our strategy of armed struggle there is town blockade as such, and then also the encirclement of towns, and so on and so forth. We never referred to actions against towns and operating against civilians in towns, but a blockade is referred to, fighting within an encirclement under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, from a military point of view, bearing in mind all the circumstances involved at that time in the autumn of 1991, from a military point of view could Dubrovnik have been taken if that had been the intention?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. According to the forces we had in November 1991, from the 6th of November onwards, around Dubrovnik including the brigade, the 472nd Brigade and the units that came to replace it, there were about 10.000 men there altogether with very strong artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in Dubrovnik and in its immediate vicinity, had there not been any armed formations there that were firing at the 2nd Operational Group would you and your units have taken any action against the town and, generally speaking, the municipality of Dubrovnik in the broadest sense? Would it have been necessary at all to take any kind of action?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. There would have been no tactical or operative need or military necessity to carry out any kind of action against a town from which there was no threat for us. That would not have made any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could Dubrovnik have been an open city?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There is this institute, so to speak, of an open city in warfare until then. When a city is declared an open city, then there is no action taken against that city. But then there should be no action taken from that city either. There were such cases in the history of warfare, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This term, an "open city," does it mean a demilitarised city as well? Is that what that term denotes as well, the absence of any military activity?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the core of the issue, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, then, who wanted to have a war around Dubrovnik? Was it the JNA or the Croatian military and political authorities?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a speculative question, and it would be something for the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was just about to make the very same point, Ms. Somers. Thank you. The admiral's opinion about that is not going to help the Chamber, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, do you agree with me when I say that it was possible to avoid all military operations around Dubrovnik had Dubrovnik been proclaimed an open city as provided for by international law and understood by international law?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That is a speculative question calling for an opinion well beyond the abilities of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It is a question that I find fully difficult to comprehend myself, Mr. Rodic, and I think the substance of it is speculative.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll restate my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, could military action have been avoided around Dubrovnik if the town had been proclaimed an open city?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think there's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That doesn't cure it. Military operations around Dubrovnik could have been avoided by no end of possible matters, Mr. Rodic, such as the JNA withdrawing from the area as one example, just to show you how difficult your question is for any sort of firm base of answer. It's a highly speculative question. I think what you're trying to get at is something that will have to be left for address rather than evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I understand, Your Honour. Very well. I'll try another road to the same end.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in the spring and summer of 1991, was Dubrovnik demilitarised, a demilitarised town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't demilitarised, or, rather, a certain increase in the number of police forces began or, rather, the MUP forces began to be on the increase, and the ZNG in the Croatian municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you say the formation of the ZNG, can you tell us what those forces were, in fact, what it was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was the establishment of smaller units of the Croatian National Guards Corps and the volunteers who, from Western Herzegovina and the Neretva River valley and the broader Dalmatian region, came into Dubrovnik, as well as the weapons themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: These newly established military forces which were created in Dubrovnik, were they a legitimate military force in the still recognised -- internationally recognised SFRY or was it an illegal army or, rather, a paramilitary organisation?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There was no reference to newly established forces or military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your question is full of assumptions that are not presently the -- established by the evidence and are in fact the subject of quite disputed evidence, I think, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'll reformulate my question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I asked you about the spring and summer of 1991, and the area is Dubrovnik. Now, was Dubrovnik, during that period, a demilitarised town?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that it was not and that weapons were coming in and that more forces were coming in to the units, to the existing units. They were being reinforced. And these units were MUP. The number of men was increased, including the volunteers, as well as the Croatian National Guards Corps, the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the ZNG was established in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly. I think it was sometime in the spring at the level of Croatia. And then there was a ban, it was prohibited, and then it was accepted that those units should be incorporated into MUP, but I don't know when that was exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about 1991, that year?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And when the Croatian National Guards Corps was being set up, was it a legitimate, lawful military force in the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection. No reference to "military force" has been in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Croatian National Guards Corps has not been designated by anyone as being a non-governmental organisation. They were armed units and referred to as such in the documents we have had so far, and in the Croatian constitution as well mention is made. Now, we can ask the witness what the Croatian National Guards Corps actually was, if that will be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It may help you overcome the problem, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, could you tell us please what the Croatian National Guards Corps, the ZNG, is, what it represented at that time.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the Republic of Croatia did not have its own armed forces and there was no Territorial Defence which could be used or, rather, it existed within the SFRY, within the frameworks of the then armed forces, the armed forces of Yugoslavia, in actual fact. However, Croatia established the Croatian National Guards Corps but within the frameworks of MUP, the MUP of Croatia, as an embryo for future armed forces, for a future armed force. I think that that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: According to the constitution of the SFRY, the Croatian National Guards Corps, was it legitimate as an armed formation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The constitution of the SFRY, of course did not recognise any forces of that kind. All it recognised was the armed forces of the country and the Territorial Defence as well as volunteer units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At that point in time, the ZNG, was it a paramilitary formation, a paramilitary organisation, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was how it was treated at the level of the Supreme Command of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know which unit of the ZNG was engaged in Dubrovnik, when it arrived there and where it came from?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the 116th Brigade was established of the ZNG at that time, and later on it became the 163rd Brigade, and it came in from the region of Metkovici and Ston, Metkovic and Ston.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know which men were part of the brigade and where they had come from?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you exactly. On the basis of the scant information I had at the time, I wasn't able to draw any conclusions as to exactly which parts of the troops they were and from which area. However, I think that apart from the local population which was included into the brigade, there were also companies from the Metkovic-Ston region, and one company, I think, had come in from Ploce. At least, that was the information we had, intelligence we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, what was the JNA -- what was the JNA's position? What was it to do if a paramilitary organisation had been set up parallel to it? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean what the JNA should have done?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I mean the state and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the constitution, there would have been no tolerance for other armed units except those prescribed and stipulated by the constitution, which means that they would have had to have been disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And was that the object of the operation carried out by the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the goals was that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was it a legitimate goal, a legitimate operation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, it was. At the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know roughly - did you have any information about this - how many men bore arms in and around Dubrovnik? How men were there under arms? So I'm not talking about the JNA, I'm talking about the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The assessments were this: In the 9th Sector - that is to say I and my associates - were told that at the time when Dubrovnik was blocked from land and sea, our assessments were that there were between two-and-a-half and 3.000 armed men in total in Dubrovnik. The assessments by the 2nd Operational Group were that there were more or, rather, they thought that there were between three-and-a-half and 5.000 men, up to 5.000.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know where the command post was of this 116th Brigade of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. It was in Metkovic, and then it was moved to Dubrovnik, I assume, and then it was sent back to Metkovic when Colonel Nojko Marinovic reformed these parts which defended the town. Commander Dajdza was there too. He's mentioned as the nominal commander of those forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Everything you're talking about, does that refer to October - December 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you happen to know how many battalions the 116th ZNG formation had?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure. The normal thing would be for it to have three to four battalions, but I don't know how they were organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about the men of that 116th Brigade of the ZNG? Were they deployed in and around Dubrovnik and turned to face your forces?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that that particular brigade did not appear as a unit which operated as a brigade. To all intents and purposes, it was never operational as a brigade, or its battalions. As far as I know, it was disbanded and only certain companies were operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And when was it disbanded?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think when the Commander Dajdza was replaced. Then it was reorganised to become the 163rd, once again in Metkovic, but that is just a guess on my part. I don't have any reliable information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is that 1992 when this became the 163rd, when it was reorganised? Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know, roughly speaking, how many police forces there were in and around Dubrovnik, including the permanent police force and the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We thought that those police forces were quite considerable and that they made up more than a third of the overall forces, which would make it up to 1.000 men for the whole Dubrovnik area, all the settlements, neighbourhoods, districts from Ston to Debeli Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If we bear in mind all the forces you have just enumerated, in October, November, December 1991, was Dubrovnik militarily active?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we thought that they did have that number of forces, and of course they would be active and operational in the extent to which our forces were. So they were active as were ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know about those 11 points that are considered the JNA proposal for the demilitarisation of Dubrovnik and for the normal functioning of the town itself as well as its population?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was in the document that was entitled "A Request to Normalise Life in the town of Dubrovnik," and for its demilitarisation, and it was formulated in 11 points.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was this basically the task of the 2nd Operational Group, to demilitarise Dubrovnik, to disarm the paramilitary formations and prevent continued illegal armament?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were the requests put forth in relation to the town of Dubrovnik. Actually, they had not been planned at the outset as such, but during the operations it turned out that this was necessary in order to resolve the crisis around Dubrovnik, namely to stop further combat operations. This is what I wanted to say: The Dubrovnik operation itself and its directive did not envisage such operations from town or at the town itself. So no one gave this any thought. No one thought that that kind of thing would actually happen. At least, that's what I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the JNA directive, did it say, inter alia, the disarming of paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's what it said in the directive quite explicitly, but implicitly, yes. However, in an order, I think, it does say disarm paramilitary formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please assist us and give D44 to the witness for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Item 1 on page 1 of this directive, is that where the objectives and the tasks of the 2nd Operational Group can be seen?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the introduction under item 1 - this is the very end of the first paragraph - does it say: "Start destroying and disarming the enemy forces and be on the ready to carry on operations to Western Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they do not have the document. Could it please be placed on the ELMO. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. I think that if it says "destroy," then disarming the forces is -- I mean, it's not only disarming that is the objective, then. It is the destroying and disarming. That's why I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Let's see what it says. The operation is to be conducted in two phases. I would kindly ask you to read out what that meant.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please ask for the appropriate part to be shown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "To engage in destroying and disarming the surrounded enemy forces and to be in a state of readiness for further offensive operations in Western Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I interrupt. The interpreters are not able to see the relevant part of the document, it seems. They do not have a copy and are dependent upon the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 1, Your Honour, with your permission, paragraph 1, the last sentence in that first paragraph and then phase 1 and phase 2. So the end of paragraph 1 on page 1 and then the entire paragraphs entitled the first phase and the second phase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Let's hope we've been able to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, Mr. Jokic, whether the task of the 2nd Operational Group described in the second phase of the directive pertained to the disarming of paramilitaries in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. There is no mention of the term "paramilitary" as far as we can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the answers we got to the previous questions refer to the legitimacy of these forces in Dubrovnik, but never mind, let him tell us again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So did this surrender and disarming, did it pertain to the enemy forces in Dubrovnik as well?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the directive itself pertained to all the forces in the zone of operations from Debeli Brijeg onwards, that is to say from the border with Croatia all the way to the Neretva River, including the entire zone. There is no special reference to the actual place where the forces are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This zone that you refer to, does it include the town of Dubrovnik itself?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does. However, we did not intend to take Dubrovnik and then disarm it by entering town. We just wanted to have a blockade. That was the objective, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can an enemy be forced to surrender by way of a blockade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, let us be quite accurate. In your view were there any paramilitary formations in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have said that the initial forces of the MUP and the ZNG had been increased by volunteers and other units, and they came up to the number that I already presented as my own estimate. That was the generally prevalent estimate at the time, or, rather, it was the official estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then, the disarming of these paramilitary formations in Dubrovnik, how could it have been carried out then? In which way? What are all the ways that would be acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what we wanted to do and what we thought of, but there are different ways. Now, what we thought and how we intended to carry this out, I can tell you that if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead. Tell us.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the command of the 2nd Operational Group formulated those 11 points according to which three items were key ones. In them, it was required that on that day, the 20th -- the 28th of October, the MUP levels be reduced to the number that was there on the 1st of October, 1991. Further on, that volunteers who had come from different regions should leave town, that weapons should be surrendered, weapons that had been brought into town in the first place, and that units of the police should be at the level at which they were before the operation had started. Those were the requirements. The guarantees were supposed to be provided by the European Community because they were supposed to monitor this entire effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When we talk about this JNA proposal consisting of 11 points, did that mean that this problem would be resolved by peaceful means or, rather, that this task that the 2nd Operational Group had would be carried out by peaceful means?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, by peaceful means. That was the way to resolve that problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If the other side does not accept those 11 points or, rather, that proposal on a peaceful settlement by way of disarmament, how was it possible, then, to compel them? In which way was it possible to compel them to agree to this?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have a plan to compel them to accept these proposals. Another way would have been to take the town, and that was never in our plan, or, rather, as far as I know not in the plan of the Supreme Command or of the 2nd Operational Group, and certainly not of the sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Could this blockade from land and sea be a vehicle for carrying out this disarmament?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the blockade was conceived as an initial objective of the operation. However, the broader objective was not only to disarm these forces. That came up only later. The first objective was to bring pressure to bear through this blockade and to deblock the garrisons and barracks on the Adriatic military naval theatre of war all the way from Pula to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was it possible to force the paramilitaries in Dubrovnik to surrender their weapons without previously sealing off all entrances and exits to and from town by using appropriate arms?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it wasn't possible to carry out disarmament without a full blockade from land and sea. A blockade was a precondition for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: By enforcing a blockade from land and sea, did you then operate exactly within the context of the objectives that were given to you through the JNA directive?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Were these legitimate objectives and tasks?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My objections, if I may say so, only pertain to the structure and number of units and the weapons they had, and this was not adequate or appropriate to the task involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: By accepting JNA proposals aimed at disarmament, could further consequences have been avoided, those that occurred in the area due to combat action taken by both sides?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And who did not accept this plan on the demilitarisation of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik. That was the negotiator from their side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did anybody else have any influence, apart from the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik, regarding the acceptance or non-acceptance of these proposals that were given by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course the republican authorities. The authorities of the Republic of Croatia that finally had the last say in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the period from October to December 1991 while you were there, did you have any signals from Dubrovnik itself in terms of a positive assessment of JNA proposals or accepting the 11 points of the JNA that refer to disarmament?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some indications and certain reports sometime between the 28th or 26th of October and the 30th of October or later. But especially this period, the end of October, there were signs that there was a possibility for having this agreement made with the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik. The assessment then was that the major hindrance to that peace agreement were the extremist forces of the HOS Croatian forces, Paraga's forces, as they were called, which did not accept the surrender of weapons at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know, perhaps, in this respect regarding acceptance or non-acceptance of an agreement with the JNA, were there perhaps some conflicts within the town of Dubrovnik itself between Paraga's forces, the HOS forces, and somebody else?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was an internal clash. We actually received reports that there had been armed showdowns between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Between the representatives of the JNA and the Crisis Staff on several occasions during the period October - December 1991, was there a mention made and propositions made for the situation of Dubrovnik's disarmament of the paramilitaries to be negotiated?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there were negotiations. At the beginning, there were contacts and talks, before the operation itself while Admiral Djurovic was still alive. He had talks with the mayor, Poljanic, Mr. Poljanic. And later on, there were negotiations. When I arrived there General Ruzinovski led the negotiations twice. I attended those negotiations, and later on it was General Strugar who led the negotiations, and he set up a group, a team led by Colonel Svicevic who had -- who conducted continuous negotiations in the course of October and November and into December with the Crisis Staff of Dubrovnik, all with the aim of having a peaceful solution to the problem, the problem of weapons and to bring about a demilitarisation for the region and the town itself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In that period October, November, and December 1991, were there several cease-fires put in place precisely to enable negotiations to take place for a peaceful settlement and for the disarmament of the paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. As far as I remember, there were 16 cease-fires in all, including the 7th of December. Sixteen cease-fires, 16 truces.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it true and correct that not once during those cease-fires and the negotiations with the Dubrovnik side that the JNA proposal was not accepted to disarm the paramilitaries peacefully?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That did not come about. It didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In order to block Dubrovnik from the land, did you have to take control of all the smaller settlements and neighbourhoods in the Dubrovnik region?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was it possible to fulfil the goal from the directive, that is to say to disarm the paramilitaries without freeing communications through Konavle, without taking control of Kupari and all the smaller places in the Dubrovnik -- along the Dubrovnik Riviera?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. That was not possible unless you had control of the accesses into town and the surrounding areas; access roads and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, would you agree with me that the paramilitaries in Dubrovnik were not ready to disarm and leave Dubrovnik at all?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
